title: Three traders. Which one gets paid?
hook: Every trader here has two links. Does that mean they all earn the same?

knows: a trade needs someone linked to both the seller and the buyer
doesNotKnow: that a trader can earn only when removing it would lose a trade

misconception: The trader with the most connections earns the most.
objective: The learner can test whether a trader is essential by taking it out and counting the trades that are lost, and explain that only an essential trader can earn a profit, because a spare one has a rival that makes the same trade.

claims.text: In the stage's market, removing T1 or T2 loses no trade (2 of 2 still happen); removing T3 loses one (1 of 2), so the value created falls from $2 to $1.
claims.source: Demo.tsx trades(): brute force over seller–buyer pairs with a present trader; FULL = 2, LOST = [0, 0, 1]. Brief check in company/domains/briefs/economics.markets.md #20 (welfare loss 0, 0, 1). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own copy of trades() (brute-force matching): full 2. Without T1, T2, T3: 2, 2, 1, so lost 0, 0, 1 and value created $2, $2, $1 (readout n x (1 - 0)). The reveal's 'Without T1, 2 of 2 ... Without T3, only 1' matches, and so do the stage badges '-0 trades' and '-1 trade'.

claims.text: Every trader on the stage has two links (one seller, one buyer).
claims.source: Demo.tsx TRADERS: each trader has one seller and one buyer. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Demo.tsx TRADERS: each trader has one seller and one buyer, so two links each. Lines 104-105 draw exactly two edges per trader, which matches the reveal 'Every trader had two links'.

claims.text: Two traders competing for the same trade undercut each other until neither earns anything.
claims.source: Bertrand-style competition between traders in the trading-network model: Blume, Easley, Kleinberg and Tardos (2009), 'Trading networks with price-setting agents', Games and Economic Behavior 67(1); Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 11. Taught in second-trader-pays-the-seller. Fact-checker confirms. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Verified by derivation, not by the sources: BEKT 2009 and E&K ch. 11 were NOT opened (cornell.edu, arxiv, sciencedirect and every scholarly host I tried were unreachable through the proxy). T1 and T2 have identical links to S1 and B1. If the trader carrying the trade keeps a margin ask - bid > 0, the rival can bid a little more to S1 or ask a little less of B1 and take the trade. So in equilibrium the margin is 0: classic Bertrand competition with identical routes and continuous prices. Neither earns anything.

claims.text: T3 has no rival for its trade, so it can charge for it.
claims.source: Monopoly trader in the trading-network model (Blume, Easley, Kleinberg and Tardos 2009; Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 11). Stated as 'can charge', not as an exact profit. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Verified by derivation; sources not opened, as in c3. T3 is the only route from S2 to B2 (Demo TRADERS). Any bid in [0, 1) and ask in (bid, 1] leaves the seller and the buyer at least as well off as no trade, and no rival can undercut, so T3 can keep a positive margin. 'Can charge' is the modest form. This also covers the predict key 'T3' (the one who profits).

claims.text: In this model a trader can earn a profit only if removing it loses value for the market; being needed allows a profit but does not guarantee one.
claims.source: Theorem in Blume, Easley, Kleinberg and Tardos (2009): in equilibrium a trader makes positive profit only if it is essential to the social optimum (removing it lowers the maximum welfare). One-directional, as the brief's Edited note requires. Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 11. Fact-checker confirms the exact statement. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD, still unverified. This rests on the general theorem in Blume, Easley, Kleinberg and Tardos (2009) (in equilibrium a trader earns a positive profit only if it is essential). I could not open BEKT or E&K ch. 11: every scholarly host I tried was unreachable through the proxy. For this stage's network I re-derived it myself (c3: T1 and T2 earn 0 and are not essential; c4: T3 is essential and can profit), but the sentence says 'in this model', which is general, and a general theorem cannot be re-derived from one example. Wording is fine and one-directional; the reveal (line 74) and the footnote match the claim. Needs: a checker with access opens BEKT 2009 (GEB 67(1)) or E&K 11.4.

claims.text: The market is a simplified model with invented values: sellers value an item $0, buyers $1.
claims.source: Stage chip and reveal footnote; Demo.tsx SELLER_VALUE, BUYER_VALUE. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Demo.tsx SELLER_VALUE = 0 and BUYER_VALUE = 1. The chip reads 'Model: sellers value an item $0, buyers $1', the predict question states the same values, and the reveal footnote reads 'A simplified model with invented values.'

recall.question: Three traders all link the same seller to the same buyer, and there is no other route. In this model, which trader can earn a profit?
options: Whichever has the most other links
recall.why: Take any one out and the other two still make the trade, so none is essential. Rivals for the same trade undercut each other to zero.
